questions.topic: Why the Romberg table beats its first column

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Order of convergence of the secant method
questions.learningObjective: state the rate at which the secant method gains accuracy
questions.stem: Compared with Newton's method, the secant method converges at a slower rate per iteration but needs no derivative. What is that rate usually described as, and what does the description mean?

options.text: Superlinear, with an order of about 1.618, meaning the number of correct digits roughly multiplies by that factor each step
Quadratic, with an order of 2, meaning the error is squared at every step, exactly as in Newton's method
options.misconception: assigns Newton's rate to the secant method, which the two-point approximation does not achieve

options.text: Linear, with an order of 1, meaning the error falls by a constant factor each step, just as in bisection
options.misconception: confuses a sublinear rate that still accelerates with a constant-factor one

options.text: Cubic, with an order of 3, since a chord is a better approximation to a curve than a tangent is
options.misconception: invents an order above the quadratic one that a two-point method cannot reach

questions.explanation: The secant method replaces the derivative by a two-point difference quotient, which is only first-order accurate in the step size, and that loss of a power is exactly why the convergence order drops from 2 to about 1.618, the golden ratio. The description of the order as a multiplier of correct digits is the useful one: the number of correct digits grows by a factor of 1.618 at each step instead of doubling, so the method still accelerates and still beats bisection, whose single extra digit per step corresponds to an order of 1. The reason the order is the golden ratio rather than some other constant is that it is the fixed point of the error recursion, in which the new error is the previous error raised to that power times a constant.

questions.stem: An iteration x to the power n plus 1 equal to g of x to the power n is used to solve an equation x equals g of x. What local condition on g guarantees that the iteration actually converges to a nearby fixed point?

options.text: The derivative of g at the fixed point is 0, so a step is not amplified at all rather than merely kept below one
options.misconception: insists on a zero derivative when a contraction already suffices

options.text: The magnitude of the derivative of g at the fixed point is less than 1, so a step is not amplified as it is passed on
The derivative of g at the fixed point is at least 1, so a step grows and pushes the iterate past the fixed point
options.misconception: inverts the condition, describing divergence as the criterion for convergence

options.text: The fixed point must be unique on the whole real line, which is what the derivative condition is used to establish
options.misconception: turns a local derivative test into a claim of global uniqueness without an interval hypothesis

questions.explanation: Near a fixed point the iteration behaves like the linear map sending an error e to e times the derivative of g at the fixed point, because the higher-order terms vanish there. If the magnitude of that derivative is less than 1, each error is smaller than the one before, so the sequence shrinks geometrically onto the fixed point. If it exceeds 1, each error is amplified and the sequence is pushed away, which is divergence. A derivative of exactly 1 is the borderline and needs more information, since the behaviour then depends on the higher-order terms. The condition is local, so it certifies convergence to a fixed point that is near the starting value and says nothing about fixed points elsewhere, which is why a separate interval argument is needed to claim uniqueness.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: state what a contraction condition guarantees about the number of fixed points
questions.stem: Suppose g is continuous on a closed interval and maps that interval into itself, and the magnitude of its derivative is at most a number strictly between 0 and 1 throughout the interval. What does that hypothesis guarantee about the equation x equals g of x?

options.text: It guarantees that the equation has at least one solution, but says nothing about how many there are
options.misconception: drops the uniqueness that the contraction hypothesis is chiefly used to establish

options.text: It guarantees that iteration converges, but only if the starting value is chosen close enough to the solution
options.misconception: adds a locality requirement that the interval hypothesis has already removed

options.text: It guarantees that the equation has exactly one solution in the interval, and that iteration from any point of the interval converges to it
It guarantees nothing, because a contraction on an interval need not have a fixed point in that interval
options.misconception: denies the existence conclusion that follows from mapping the interval into itself

questions.explanation: Two conclusions come from the two halves of the hypothesis, and both are needed. Continuity together with the fact that g maps the interval into itself gives existence: at one endpoint the function x minus g of x is at least zero and at the other it is at most zero, so the intermediate value theorem supplies a solution. The bound on the derivative, with its magnitude strictly below 1, gives uniqueness, because two distinct solutions a and b would have to satisfy the difference of a and b equal to the difference of g at a and g at b, whose magnitude is at most that constant times the magnitude of the difference, an impossibility. The same contraction constant then makes the iteration converge from any point of the interval, since two successive iterates are always within that factor of each other. This is the standard fixed-point theorem, and it is the reason a good rearrangement of an equation is worth the effort of finding.
questions.hint: Split the hypothesis into the part that gives existence and the part that rules out a second solution, and then note what the contraction factor does to successive iterates.

questions.topic: Round-off limits the usable step size
questions.learningObjective: explain why shrinking the step eventually destroys a difference quotient
questions.stem: A student estimates the derivative of a smooth function by a central difference with a very small step and finds the answer growing steadily less accurate as the step shrinks. What is happening, and why does it set a floor under the usable step size?

options.text: The truncation error of the central difference grows as the step shrinks, so the estimate must deteriorate for small steps
options.misconception: inverts the behaviour, since the truncation error of a central difference falls as the square of the step

options.text: The function stops being differentiable at the finer sampling points, so the difference quotient has nothing to converge to
options.misconception: claims a loss of differentiability that the smoothness hypothesis rules out

questions.explanation: Two errors compete. The truncation error of a central difference falls as the square of the step, so making the step smaller always helps that term. The round-off error behaves in the opposite way: the function values are each known only to a fixed relative precision, so their difference carries an absolute error of roughly that precision, and dividing by the step multiplies that error by the reciprocal of the step. The total therefore has a minimum at a step of order the cube root of the relative precision, for a central difference, and improving on that requires higher precision rather than a smaller step. The same effect is why a difference quotient is a poor way to compute a small derivative and why an analytic or symbolic derivative is preferred whenever one is available.

questions.topic: What each quadrature rule is exact for
questions.learningObjective: compare the degrees of exactness of the three standard rules
questions.stem: Compare the midpoint rule, the trapezoid rule and Simpson's rule by the degree of the polynomial each one reproduces exactly on a panel, by the power of the panel width in its leading error term, and by the direction in which it errs on a curve that bends upward. Use worked examples to support each of the three claims.

answer.exemplar: The three rules differ in what they construct on a panel and then integrate exactly. The midpoint rule evaluates the integrand at the centre of a panel and multiplies by the panel width, which is exactly the integral of the constant polynomial through that single sample, so it is exact for degree 0. The trapezoid rule replaces the curve on a panel by the straight line through the two endpoint values and integrates that line, so it is exact for degree 1. Simpson's rule fits a cubic through four sample values over two panels and integrates that cubic, so it is exact for degree 3, which is a jump of two degrees rather than one. The worked checks are simple: the midpoint rule and the trapezoid rule both return 2.5 for the integral of 3x plus 1 over 0 to 1, where the exact value is 2.5, while for the integral of x squared over 0 to 1 the exact value is one third, the midpoint rule with one panel returns 0.25 and the trapezoid rule with one panel returns 0.5, both wrong, whereas Simpson's rule with two subintervals returns exactly one third. The error terms follow from the degrees of exactness by a Taylor argument: a rule exact to degree d has a leading error proportional to the panel width to the power d plus 1, because the leading term it fails to reproduce is the one of degree d plus 1. So the midpoint error falls as the square of the panel width, the trapezoid error also falls as the square, and the Simpson error falls as the fourth power. The observed behaviour matches exactly: for x squared over 0 to 1 the trapezoid errors with 1, 2 and 4 panels are 0.1666667, 0.0416667 and 0.0104167, each a quarter of the one before, and for x to the fourth over 0 to 1 the Simpson errors with 2, 4 and 8 subintervals are 0.0083333, 0.0005208 and 0.0000326, each about one sixteenth of the one before. The third feature, the direction of the error, comes from the geometry of the approximating shape. On a curve that is concave up, the midpoint rectangle is inscribed, so it lies under the curve and the rule underestimates; the trapezoid chord is circumscribed, so it lies above the curve and the rule overestimates; and Simpson's fitted cubic is a better approximation than either, though on a quartic it also overestimates, returning 0.2005208 against an exact 0.2. The two-sided character of the midpoint and trapezoid rules is what makes them useful together, since the true value always lies between them whenever the integrand is concave up on every panel, and their average is already better than either one alone. That pairing is the first line of the Romberg table, and the factor of 4 by which their errors differ is what makes the cancellation exact.

questions.explanation: The exemplar has to show the three degrees of exactness with concrete computed checks, connect each degree to the matching power of the panel width in the error, and demonstrate the error directions with actual numbers, because a reader who has only memorised the table of orders will not see why the exponents match. The final sentence earns its place by showing that the comparison is not merely descriptive but the source of the extrapolation that follows from it.
